To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the denotational semantics of a functional language with countably infinite nondeterminism can be given in a domain that is a bidomain (a domain with two bottom elements), and that this bidomain can be used to prove full abstraction for the language.

the semantics of nondeterministic programs is not well defined without a notion of randomness, and that the notion of a random number generator is essential for defining such semantics in a way that is fully abstract with regard to testing.

the denotational semantics of a sequential functional language can be defined in terms of bidomains, that this semantics is fully abstract with re-spect to may- and must-testing, and that the semantics of the language with random number gen-eration can be defined in the same way as the semantics of the original language.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the semantics of programs which exhibit nondeterminism in a way that cannot be captured by a finite set of possible outcomes, and with the development of fully abstract denotational semantics of languages which exhibit such nondeterminism.
the following problem:  How can we describe the semantics of a nondeterministic functional language with random numbers in a fully abstract way?
the semantics of programs that exhibit nondeterministic behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the theory is a fully abstract denotational semantics.
the theory is a good candidate for a theory of the real numbers.
the language is fully abstract with repect to may-and-mus testing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have extended the domain-theoretic approach to full abstraction to the countable nondeterminism.

we have developed the theory of bidomains, which are a generalization of the well-studied notion of dcpo (directed-complete partial order), and used them to construct a denotational model for the nondeterministic language, where we prove full abstraction for both may-and-must equivalence.
we have developed a denotational framework for countable nondeterminism, and proved its full abstraction with respect to may and must testing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the standard approach for defining denotational semantics, which is to interpret types as sets, is not suitable for countable nondeterminism.
, for a language with nondeterministic input, it is necessary and sufficient to consider bidomain semantics in order to achieve full abstraction.

, while it is not possible to fully abstract a countably infinite nondeterministic language with a domain model that is a countable union of countable nondeterministic sets, it is possible with a bidomain model that combines countable and nondeterministic information.
